name: Secrets management
summary: A locked vault for passwords, keys and tokens, handed out at runtime.
howItWorks: A secrets manager stores credentials encrypted and hands them only to callers whose identity is allowed to read them. Apps fetch secrets at startup or on demand instead of keeping them in code or config files. Every read is audited, and many managers rotate credentials automatically, changing the database password and the stored value together.
analogy: A hotel safe with an access log. Only the right keycard opens it, every opening is recorded, and the combination changes on a schedule.
useWhen: Database passwords, API keys, signing keys, certificates
Auditing who read which secret, and when
Finding secrets that leaked into code, wikis or chat anyway, with a scanner such as GitHub secret scanning, gitleaks, TruffleHog or HCP Vault Radar
avoidWhen: Committing secrets to git, even in a private repository
Baking secrets into images or printing them in CI logs
example: The API’s role is allowed to read `db/password`, so it fetches the current value on boot. Every 30 days the manager rotates the database password. A script on someone’s laptop with no role is refused.

diagram.caption: The app, running with an allowed role, gets the secret. The laptop script has no permission and is refused. Periodically the manager rotates the database password.

story: For a long time a database password lived wherever the code that needed it lived: in source code, in configuration files, in configuration management, or copied onto servers by hand. When Square open-sourced its own secrets tool in 2015, its engineers listed what was wrong with that. Source repositories exposed secrets to developers and CI systems that never needed them, hand-deployed secrets were scattered and impossible to audit, and configuration management tools, built to keep everything visible with full history, were exactly the wrong place for them.

The Twelve-Factor App methodology gave a simple test: could the codebase be made open source at any moment without compromising any credentials? Its answer was environment variables. Dedicated secret managers went further. In April 2015 Square released Keywhiz, which hands secrets to services as files over mutual TLS, and HashiCorp announced Vault, which also creates credentials on demand for each client and revokes them when their lease ends. In April 2018 AWS launched Secrets Manager with automatic rotation; until then, it noted, customers had to run extra infrastructure just to manage secrets.

Since then the push has been to need fewer stored secrets at all. GitHub began scanning public repositories for leaked tokens in 2018, and short-lived identity tokens, such as GitHub Actions’ OIDC tokens in 2021, let workloads reach clouds without any stored key.

choices.choice: Keep secrets out of code and config files
choices.why: Anything committed to a repository is exposed to everyone and every system that can read it, including CI, and config files are easy to commit by mistake. Storing secrets separately means code can be shared without sharing access.

choices.choice: Fetch at runtime, authorized by identity
choices.why: A central store that checks who is asking and logs every read answers the question scattered config files never could: who has access to this secret, and who used it?
A secret that never changes stays useful to an attacker forever. Automatic rotation limits that window, and dynamic secrets that expire within hours shrink it further.

timeline.text: Square open-sources Keywhiz; HashiCorp announces Vault, both in April
AWS Secrets Manager launches in April with automatic rotation
GitHub starts scanning public repositories for leaked tokens
GitHub Actions OIDC lets CI deploy to clouds without stored keys
Vault 2.0 syncs secrets using workload identity, without static credentials
